rows.title: Pupil
rows.text: If you are a red fox or an arctic fox, your pupil is a narrow vertical slit. If you are a gray fox, your pupil is oval, unlike the slits of foxes in the genus Vulpes, such as the red fox.
rows.note: Left out R4-R13: their quotes are classification codes that do not state the pupil shape. R13 (island fox, "Vertical") also conflicts with R1 for the genus Urocyon, so I did not describe island, Tibetan sand or Rüppell's foxes.

rows.title: Sharpest spot
rows.text: If you are a red fox or an Arctic fox, the back of each eye has one small spot, called the area centralis, where the cells that send signals to the brain are packed most tightly. A red fox also has a moderate band of dense cells across the retina, and an Arctic fox's spot is packed more tightly than a red fox's. Nobody has measured this spot in the other foxes.
rows.note: Left out R3's "prominent visual streak" for the Arctic fox because its quote does not state it; R1 (dog) not used since it is a different genus.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: If you are a red fox or an arctic fox, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. Most of yours sense middle to long wavelengths of light and a minority sense short wavelengths, which makes your color vision dichromatic. Nobody has counted these cells in a gray fox or an island fox.
rows.note: Left out the 555 nm peak (R1-R3): its quote says "one cone pigment", which does not match two cone classes, and the number had no job.

rows.title: Night eyes
rows.text: On many nights, the natural light outdoors is brighter than the dimmest light that a coyote can see, as shown in a test with three coyotes. Coyotes are relatives of yours, but nobody has measured how little light you need to see.
rows.note: Only a coyote record exists, and absolute sensitivity does not carry between genera, so the row stays at i and names the coyote result without applying it to foxes.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's, who reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a red fox, the density of nerve cells in your retina gives an estimate of about 6 cycles a degree, and if you are an arctic fox, about 9. Of the other foxes, nobody has measured how sharply they see.
rows.note: Both fox figures are anatomical estimates, not eye-chart tests; the row says so. Gray and island fox are unmeasured, and Vulpes relatives are covered only by the general closing line.

rows.title: Hearing
rows.text: If you are a red fox, you hear tones from about 50 hertz up to about 48,000 hertz, a span of almost 10 octaves. That comes from hearing tests with three red foxes, and nobody has measured the hearing of the other kinds of fox.
rows.note: No record gives a human hearing range, so the row makes no comparison with a human.
